title: 20 EMA Pullback
teaches: The 20 EMA pullback as we trade it: a leader in a rising trend, above its 200-day with the 20 EMA over a rising 50-day, drifts quietly back to the rising 20 EMA, a session holds the line, the buy is a cent over that session's high at market in regular hours, the stop sits a few cents under its low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: the odds are very high that when a security makes a new momentum high and pulls back, it will retest its recent high. Therefore, any pullback from a new momentum high can be bought.
facts.claim: Raschke on the Holy Grail: after a new momentum high the odds are very high a pullback retests the recent high, so any such pullback can be bought.

facts.quote: 2. Look for a retracement in price to the 20 period exponential moving average. This will usually be accompanied by a turndown in the ADX.
facts.claim: Raschke's rule: look for a retracement to the 20-period exponential moving average.

facts.quote: 3. When the price touches the 20 period moving average, put a buy stop above the high of the previous bar.
facts.claim: Raschke's buy: a buy stop above the high of the previous bar once price touches the 20-period average.

facts.quote: 4. Once filled, enter a protective sell stop at the newly formed swing low. Trail stops as profits grow.
facts.claim: Raschke's stop: the newly formed swing low, trailed as profits grow.

facts.quote: This is a case where there is no reason to be in this trade.
facts.claim: Raschke on a pullback buy that showed little movement for five days: no reason to be in the trade.

facts.quote: On the 30-minute time frame, the ADX rose above 30, so we’ll buy the first retrace-ment to the 20-period EMA and look to exit on a push to new highs.
facts.claim: Raschke buys the first retracement to the 20-period EMA after a strong trend.

facts.quote: I use market orders most of the time.
facts.claim: Raschke uses market orders most of the time.

facts.quote: By focusing on the 10 and 20-day exponential moving averages (EMAs), you can identify key moments to buy stocks when the price dips into these levels after a strong rally.
facts.claim: Kell: buy the dip into the 10 and 20-day EMAs after a strong rally.

facts.quote: But always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in before making your trade.
facts.claim: Kell: always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in.

facts.quote: The EMA Crossback refers to the first time the stock price retests its moving averages after a strong upward move, called a “Wedge Pop.”
facts.claim: Kell: the EMA Crossback is the first retest of the averages after a Wedge Pop.

facts.quote: The EMA Crossback works best when the price gently moves sideways, allowing the moving averages to rise to the price.
facts.claim: Kell: the pullback works best when price drifts sideways and the rising averages catch up.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price “surfs” the rising 10- and 20-day. and sometimes toe 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a leader surfs its rising 10 and 20-day lines and sometimes toes the 50-day.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day, no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: A big move higher sometime in the past 1-3 months. This move can be anywhere from 30-100%+ and usually lasts a few days to a few weeks.
facts.claim: Kullamagi wants a big move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months first.

facts.quote: If a beginner stick to the 10-day. You wait for the first CLOSE below the 10- day.
facts.claim: Kullamagi trails the 10-day and sells on the first close below it.

facts.quote: As long as the price remains above the 21-day EMA, any short-term movements can be considered noise, rather than a clear signal of a change in trend.
facts.claim: Keller: above the 21-day EMA, short-term moves are noise, not a change of trend.

facts.quote: The price is above the 21-day EMA, the 21-day is above the 50-day SMA, and the 50-day is above the 200-day SMA.
facts.claim: Keller's proper order: price over the 21-day EMA, over the 50-day, over the 200-day.

facts.quote: I think of the 21-day EMA as the first line of defense, an initial stop within an uptrend phase.
facts.claim: Keller calls the 21-day EMA the first line of defense in an uptrend.

facts.quote: chasing stocks hitting a new high in price can be the surest way to frustration

facts.quote: a moving average gives you a reason to study price action closely as it approaches, not a reason to act automatically.

walkthroughs.title: GE, January 2024: the low kisses the line
steps: GE in January 2024, a leader in an uptrend. It drifts back four days to its rising 20 EMA on light volume.
January 4 the low kisses the line to the cent and closes above it. It's over the 50-day and 200-day too.
January 5 it trades a cent over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 100.39. Stop just under the hold low, 99.07.
A slice back through the line that takes the low says it's wrong. Instead, 3R in 5 sessions. Sell some into it.

walkthroughs.title: NVDA, May 2023: the textbook leader, out before the report
steps: NVDA in May 2023, the textbook leader. Its 20 EMA is rising, and it rests four days on light volume.
May 12 holds the line and closes above it. May 15 it clears that high. Buy at market, 28.79. Stop 28.02.
3R in 3 sessions, a fair spot for a first sell. The day before the report it's up 3.9R.
Hold through a report only if you're up 5R. At 3.9R you sell before it, even on a chart this good.

walkthroughs.title: CRM, June 2020: the shallow shakeout
steps: Watch the line on CRM, June 2020. A four-day pullback on light volume, then the low dips just under the 20 EMA.
Same session, it closes back above the line. That's a shakeout, not a lost line. The hold is in.
June 30 it trades a cent over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 183.72. Stop just under the hold low, 179.97.
A second close under the line before the trigger would kill it. Instead, 3R in 2 sessions, and you hold.

questions.q: What setup are you looking at here?
choices: A leader resting on its rising 20 EMA
A stock sliding under a falling 20 EMA
A tight range under a flat ceiling
A sharp V-bottom off the 200-day
questions.answer: A leader resting on its rising 20 EMA
questions.why: That's a 20 EMA pullback. A leader ran, then drifted back to a line that's still rising, and a session held it. The trend never broke. Price just came back to meet the average. Now look at the last candle. A hammer and an inside day, sitting right on the line. That's a good look. The buy comes when a later session trades over its high. Your stop goes a few cents under that session's low, so the risk stays small. A falling line, or a stock living under it, is a different story.
questions.lesson_line: A leader pulls in, the line's still rising, a session holds it. That's the setup.

wrong.A sharp V-bottom off the 200-day: A V off the 200-day is a reversal. This stock never broke its trend, it just pulled in.
wrong.A stock sliding under a falling 20 EMA: That's a downtrend. We want a leader, and a line that's still pointing up.
wrong.A tight range under a flat ceiling: That's a flat base. Price rests under a level there. Here it dips to a moving line.

questions.simple: It's a strong stock resting on a rising 20 EMA. That line gives us a spot to buy with a small stop.

deeper.example: GE, January 2024: four days back to its 20 EMA on 0.78x volume. The low kissed the line to the cent. That's the shape of the setup.
deeper.counter: Keller calls this line the first line of defense in an uptrend. Kullamagi has his leaders surf their rising 10 and 20-day lines.

reasons: card numbers are proposed, not rulings
several facts agree

questions.story: Here's the chart. Check the trend, the last few bars, and the lines they're sitting on.

questions.q: Which line does price have to be above before we buy any stock?
choices: The 200-day simple average
The 50-day, if it's rising
The 9 EMA, closing back over it
None, the touch is enough
questions.why: The 200-day. Under it we don't buy stocks, period. That's a hard line for us. Above it the big trend is up, so a dip to the 20 EMA is more likely a rest than the start of a reversal. Under it the stock is in a downtrend, and what looks like a pullback is really just a bounce. So you check the 200-day first, then you look at the touch and the hold.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day there's no pullback to buy, just a bounce.

wrong.The 9 EMA, closing back over it: Getting back over the 9 EMA is a nice sign. It's not the line that decides.
wrong.The 50-day, if it's rising: The 50-day matters, and we like it rising. But the hard line is the 200-day.
wrong.None, the touch is enough: The touch is the pattern. The 200-day comes before any of that.

questions.simple: The 200-day. Below it we don't buy stocks, because a dip there is more likely a bounce in a downtrend.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B26

questions.story: A leader just held its rising 20 EMA and closed above it. Before you look at the touch, check where price sits against the big averages.

deeper.counter: Brian Shannon says it this way: above the 200-day, the larger trend is innocent until proven guilty.

questions.q: You buy a 20 EMA pullback. Your stop goes a few cents under the low of the session that held the line.
questions.why: True. That session's low is where the hold either works or it doesn't. If price trades under it, the buyers who defended the line are gone, and so are you, with a small loss. Not right on it, though. Price loves to tick an exact low and turn. Those few cents keep normal noise from taking you out. It's our go-to low of the day (LOD) stop, taken from the session that held.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first. A few cents under the low of the session that held.
questions.simple: True. Under that low the hold has failed, so we're out with a small loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and F62

deeper.counter: Kullamagi sets his stop at the low of the day too, and keeps it no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The 20 EMA must be ___: higher than it was 10 sessions earlier.
questions.why: Rising. The 20 EMA must be higher than it was 10 sessions earlier. A line that flattens or turns down before entry ends the setup. Kell: the pullback works best when the rising averages catch up to the price.
questions.lesson_line: A rising line is the whole setup. A flat one is a different chart.
questions.simple: The line must be higher than it was 10 sessions ago, so the stock rests on a line that still climbs.

reasons: the 10-session test is a proposed card number

questions.q: Where does your buy go?
choices: A cent over the hold candle's high
At the close of the hold session
A limit order resting on the 20 EMA
A close back over the 9 EMA
questions.answer: A cent over the hold candle's high
questions.why: A cent over 259.85, the hold candle's high. Set an alert there tonight. When price trades through it on a later session, you buy at market. Your stop goes a few cents under 255.35, the hold low. Look at that candle too. An inside day on light volume, just above the line. Quiet, the look I want. The hold only tells you the line held. Trading over that high tells you buyers are pushing past it. Buying the close is buying before anything has happened.
questions.lesson_line: The hold candle sets the trigger. Over its high, you're in.

wrong.At the close of the hold session: The close is the hold itself. The buy waits for price to trade over that candle's high on a later session.
wrong.A limit order resting on the 20 EMA: That buys the touch before any session has held. We wait for the hold.
wrong.A close back over the 9 EMA: Getting back over the 9 EMA is a nice sign. It raises the grade. It's not the trigger.

questions.simple: A cent over 259.85, the hold candle's high, because that's when buyers prove they're pushing it up.

deeper.trap: Buying the touch before any session has held is a named mistake. Kell says to always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in. The hold candle's high is where you set the alert, and the buy happens only when it trades.

reasons: the cent-over-the-high buy is the proposed fallback trigger, held under D-003

questions.story: This leader pulled back to its rising 20 EMA. The last bar held the line and closed above it. Its high is 259.85, its low 255.35.

questions.q: Entries on a 20 EMA pullback are limit orders placed on the 20 EMA, in regular hours only.
questions.why: False. Entries are market orders, not limit orders resting on the 20 EMA. We buy in regular trading hours only, with no new buys outside them. Raschke is one voice on this: I use market orders most of the time.
questions.lesson_line: Market order the moment it trades. Regular hours only.
questions.simple: False, because we enter with market orders in regular hours, not limit orders resting on the line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E57 and E58

questions.q: The trend is strong, so you can buy the first touch of the 20 EMA before any session has held it.
questions.why: False. A moving average isn't a wall. Stocks slice right through it all the time. The touch only tells you price got there. A session that holds the line and closes above it, that's your proof buyers showed up. So I wait for it, even if it costs me a little price. Buying the touch is a named mistake, and a strong trend doesn't change that.
questions.lesson_line: The line is a place to watch, not a place to buy. Let a session hold it.
questions.simple: False. A touch only shows price got there, so we wait for a session to hold the line first.

reasons: the never-before-hold rule is a proposed card line
if D-003 moves the buy to the hold session itself, the wording may need a re-read

deeper.counter: Shannon puts it well: a moving average is a reason to study price closely as it approaches, not a reason to act automatically.

questions.q: During the pullback the session's low reaches under the 50-day SMA. Which card is it now, if anything?
choices: The 50-day MA pullback
Still the 20 EMA pullback
A Remount of the 50-day
A bull flag on the 50-day
questions.why: The 50-day form of the moving-average pullback, if anything. The 20 EMA pullback needs the hold session's low to stay above the 50-day SMA. Once the low reaches the 50-day, the 50-day is the line, and it is judged on its own card.
questions.lesson_line: Name the line the low touched. The 50-day is a different card.

wrong.Still the 20 EMA pullback: The 20 EMA pullback's low holds above the 50-day. This low went through it.
wrong.A Remount of the 50-day: A Remount is a line lost and retaken, not a dip. One session's low under the 50-day is not that.
wrong.A bull flag on the 50-day: A flag needs a pole. The question here is only which line the low touched.

questions.simple: The 50-day pullback, because the low went down to the 50-day, so that is the line that was tested.

reasons: the 50-day boundary is a proposed card line
fixed before

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card, the pullback lasts 2 to ___ sessions from the swing high to the hold session.
questions.why: 15. The card says the pullback lasts 2 to 15 sessions from the swing high to the hold session. Our examples ran 4 to 10 sessions, such as TOL's 10-day drift. A drift past 15 sessions does not fit this card.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions: two to fifteen on our card.
questions.simple: On our card a pullback may last at most 15 sessions, counted from the swing high to the hold session.

deeper.example: TOL in 2004 drifted 10 days down to the line on 0.69x volume and reached 3R in 6 sessions. GE took only 4 days. Both fit the 2 to 15 session window, so the cap is a limit, not a target.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c04)
the 2 to 15 length is a proposed number that may change; other dossiers say 2 to 8 and 2 to 10
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Read the red days and the volume on the way down. What's that telling you?
choices: Small red days and volume drying up
A few big red days on rising volume
One huge red day into the line
A gap down through the 50-day
questions.answer: Small red days and volume drying up
questions.why: Small red days, and volume dries up into the line. That's what I want to see. The people who own it aren't rushing for the exit, so the line has a better shot at holding. That raises the grade. Our grade, A+ down to B-, is our call on how clean a setup is, and it sets your size. A heavy red day wouldn't kill it. It'd be a warning and a lower grade. ILMN went on to reach 3R in 10 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet drift, small bars, volume dries up. That's the look I want.

wrong.A few big red days on rising volume: That's sellers pressing. It doesn't kill the setup, but it's a warning and a lower grade.
wrong.A gap down through the 50-day: Once it's through the 50-day, it's not a 20 EMA pullback anymore.
wrong.One huge red day into the line: One big flush is a sell-off, not a quiet rest. That knocks the grade down.

questions.simple: Small red days and volume drying up. Little selling means the line is more likely to hold, and that raises the grade.

reasons: rests on the settled HEAVY-DOWN ruling (2026-11-14)
the 1.5x line is a card number

questions.story: This leader drifts six days back to its rising 20 EMA, and the last bar holds the line.

questions.q: A stock drifting along its 20 EMA, no swing high at least 1 ATR above the hold low, has not pulled back.
questions.why: True. The card needs the pullback to be at least 1 ATR off the swing high. That is measured from the highest high of the last 11 sessions to the hold session's low. A stock sliding along the line with no such dip has nothing to pull back from.
questions.lesson_line: You need something to pull back from. Measure the dip in ATR.
questions.simple: True, because the card needs a dip of at least 1 ATR from the swing high before it counts as a pullback.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c03)
the 1 ATR depth and the 11 session window are proposed numbers
tied to held decision D-029
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Which low counts as a touch by the card?
choices: Low of 51.00
A low of 48.30
Low of 47.90
Low of 46.00
questions.why: A low of 48.30. The touch band runs from 0.25 ATR above the 20 EMA to 1 ATR below it. With an ATR of 2.00, 48.30 is under the line by less than one ATR. The line gets run through; it is not a wall.
questions.lesson_line: A touch has a band: a little above the line, up to one ATR under it.

wrong.Low of 51.00: That low stayed more than 0.25 ATR above the line. It never came down to touch it.
wrong.Low of 47.90: That is under the line by more than one ATR of 2.00. It went through the touch band, not into it.
wrong.Low of 46.00: That is far more than one ATR under the line. The line gets run through, but not by that much.

questions.story: Four stocks each have a 20 EMA at 50.00 and an ATR of 2.00. Each closes above the line today, but their lows differ.
questions.simple: A low of 48.30, because it is under the line by less than one ATR, which is inside the touch band.

reasons: the touch band is a proposed card number
key rests on a comparison

questions.q: If the pullback keeps closing under the 20 EMA, the line is lost and the setup is off.
questions.why: True. Closes that keep sitting under the 20 EMA mean the line is lost. The setup is off until it sets up again. One shakeout that is reclaimed the next session can still be a hold. How deep a dip may go, and how fast it must come back, is a judgment call, not a fixed number.
questions.lesson_line: One shakeout can be fine. Closes that stay under the line mean it is lost.
questions.simple: True, because closes that stay under the 20 EMA mean the line is lost, and we wait for a new setup.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c14)
the two closes and 0.5 ATR lines are proposed numbers
tied to held decision D-036
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: A scanner puts the stop at the line minus 1 ATR. Why is that not our stop?
choices: Too wide; use the day's low
Too wide only for slow movers
Too tight; it sits inside the noise
Too tight; use the 50-day instead
questions.answer: Too wide; use the day's low
questions.why: Too wide. The line minus 1 ATR is wider than 1 ATR whenever the entry is above the line. Our stop is a few cents under the hold session's low, and it is a real order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is a price under a candle, not a line minus a cushion.

wrong.Too tight; it sits inside the noise: It is the other way round: a cushion under the line is wider than the day's low, not tighter.
wrong.Too wide only for slow movers: The line minus 1 ATR is wider than 1 ATR whenever the entry is above the line, for any mover.
wrong.Too tight; use the 50-day instead: The line minus 1 ATR is wider, not tighter. And our stop is not the 50-day: it is a price a few cents under the hold session's low.

questions.simple: It is too wide, because our stop goes just under the low of the hold session instead.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3 and F62

questions.q: Your initial stop can be a close under the 20 EMA that you watch for, as long as you act on it.
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. A close under a line cannot sit with the broker as an order, so it cannot be the initial stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False, because a stop must be a real order with the broker and a close under a line cannot be one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook D41

questions.q: How do you want the 20 EMA sitting against the 50-day?
choices: Above a rising 50-day SMA
Above a falling 50-day SMA
Below the 50-day, catching up
Crossing it that session
questions.why: Above a 50-day that's rising too. That's the picture of a leader resting. The trend is up on the short average and on the medium one, so the dip is a rest inside a trend that's working. A 20 EMA under the 50-day is a stock still repairing. A falling 50-day says the bigger move is tired. Neither one is where I want to be buying the line.
questions.lesson_line: The 20 EMA over a rising 50-day. Get that right, then look at the dip.

wrong.Below the 50-day, catching up: A 20 EMA under the 50-day is a stock in repair, not a leader resting.
wrong.Crossing it that session: A cross is the trend changing sides. We want that order already settled.
wrong.Above a falling 50-day SMA: A falling 50-day means the medium trend isn't up. We want it climbing under the 20 EMA.

questions.simple: Above a rising 50-day. Both trends point up, so the dip is a rest, not a repair.

reasons: the 20-over-50 order is a proposed card line, not the owner's B26

questions.story: Here's the hold session. Find the 20 EMA and the 50-day on the chart.

deeper.counter: Keller's proper order stacks price over the fast EMA, the fast EMA over the 50-day, and the 50-day over the 200-day.

questions.q: It taps the flat line today. Do you buy it?
choices: No, the line has stopped rising
Yes, the touch is what counts
Yes, a late tap is the strongest
Yes, four months up proves it
questions.answer: No, the line has stopped rising
questions.why: Pass. The whole point of this setup is a leader resting on a line that's still climbing. The rising line is what lifts price off the tap. When it goes flat after a four-month run, the move that carried the stock is getting tired. Now the tap has nothing under it. NVDA gave us this exact look after a four-month run. The buy stopped out on day 1, and a month later it was still under the 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: A tired line doesn't hold. Pass on the tap of a flat 20 EMA.

wrong.Yes, the touch is what counts: The touch is just the pattern. The line has to be rising first.
wrong.Yes, a late tap is the strongest: A late tap on a flat line is the weak one. The trend under it has tired.
wrong.Yes, four months up proves it: A past run isn't support. What matters is the line right now, and it's flat.

questions.story: A leader has run for four months. Its 20 EMA has stopped rising and gone flat. Price drifts down into it, and today it taps the line.
questions.simple: No. A flat line means the trend is tired, so the tap has nothing to bounce off.

reasons: the flat-line test is a proposed card number

questions.q: Do you buy the trigger tomorrow?
choices: No, the report is inside 3 days
Yes, a first tap is the best one
Yes, but only at half size
No, it needs a second hold
questions.answer: No, the report is inside 3 days
questions.why: No. We don't make new buys in the 3 days before a report. This one reports in two days, so tomorrow's trigger lands right inside that window. Here's the risk. A report can gap the stock straight through your stop, and a stop can't catch an overnight gap. You'd be sitting in a size built for a tight stop with a gap you can't control. Let it report. If it still sets up after, it can hold the line again and you buy that.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report. Let it report, then look again.

wrong.Yes, a first tap is the best one: The tap is fine. The report inside 3 days is the problem.
wrong.Yes, but only at half size: A smaller buy is still a new buy inside the window. Size doesn't fix a gap.
wrong.No, it needs a second hold: One session holding the line is enough. You pass because of the report.

questions.story: A leader taps its rising 20 EMA for the first time. Today the session holds and closes above the line. The company reports in two days, after the close.
questions.simple: No. Earnings can gap it past our stop overnight, so we wait until the report is out.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h08)
rests on the owner's rulebook B22; whether the 3 days are sessions or calendar days is held under D-072

questions.q: Bought the hold at 147.30 with the stop at 145.05. Where is 3R?
questions.why: One R is the fill minus the stop, 147.30 minus 145.05. Add three of those to the fill: 147.30 plus 3 times (147.30 minus 145.05) is 154.05. 3R is a yardstick, not a fixed sale point.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a yardstick, and the first sell is a judgment.
questions.simple: 3R sits at 154.05, which is the fill plus three times the stop distance.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h05)

questions.simple: Sell a big part. A climax run is when a big gain is easiest to bank, while buyers are eager.

deeper.trap: A climax run feels like proof the trade is great, so holding it all feels right. Sell a big part into it. The exact size is your judgment, but the call is to sell.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h16)
rests on the owner's rulebook C34, a judgment call

questions.q: Your plan says sell some at 5R. The stock gaps open at 5.4R. You have to sell at the open.
questions.why: False. A gap past a profit level isn't an automatic sale. Selling part into the open is one option, and it's a judgment. Think about why. A stock that gaps up strong on its own is showing you demand, and it can keep running. So watch how it trades. If it fades, sell into it. If it's ripping, you can let it work. Either way it's your call, not a rule.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past your level isn't an automatic sale. Watch how it trades, then decide.
questions.simple: False. A strong open can keep running, so selling into a gap is our choice, not a rule.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h25)
rests on the owner's rulebook F63

questions.q: Where does your stop go?
choices: A few cents under 93.60
Right at your entry price
A close under the 20 EMA
A flat 1% under your entry
questions.why: A few cents under 93.60. That's the low of the day, and it's lower than the hold candle's 93.88, so the stop goes under the lower one. Think about what that low means. Buyers already defended it once this morning. If price trades back under it after you bought, the dip you bought has failed, and you want out with a small loss. The stop comes from the chart. The size comes from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop goes a few cents under the lower low, today's or the hold candle's.

wrong.A close under the 20 EMA: A close under a line can't sit with the broker as an order. The stop is a price under a low.
wrong.Right at your entry price: A stop on your entry gives the trade zero room. Breakeven comes later, after it's worked.
wrong.A flat 1% under your entry: The stop comes from a low on the chart, not a percent you picked. Then you size from it.

questions.story: The hold candle's low is 93.88. Next session it dips to 93.60 first, still above the rising 20 EMA. Then it trades over the hold candle's high and you buy.
questions.simple: Under 93.60. If price breaks today's low after you bought, the dip has failed and you're out.

reasons: teaches the proposed fallback trigger, held under D-003
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Price holds the 20 EMA and the same session closes back over the 9 EMA. On our card, that 9 EMA remount is what?
choices: A confirming sign of the hold
The buy order's trigger
An invalidation of the hold
The line the stop sits at
questions.answer: A confirming sign of the hold
questions.why: A confirming sign, not a gate. On our card a close back over the 9 EMA backs up the hold. It is not the trigger, and a missing remount does not cancel the hold.
questions.lesson_line: The 9 EMA remount backs up the hold. It is not the buy.

wrong.The buy order's trigger: The Model Book playbook makes it the buy. Our card makes it a confirming sign, and the buy is the trade over the hold candle's high.
wrong.An invalidation of the hold: The card calls it a confirming sign. It does not cancel the hold.
wrong.The line the stop sits at: The stop is a few cents under the hold session's low, never a line.

questions.simple: It is a confirming sign, not a gate, so the trade can go on without it.

reasons: proposed card rule that may change
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Growing sales and earnings come first when we grade a pullback buy. The chart is just the tie-breaker.
questions.why: False. It's the other way around. The chart comes first. We like growing sales and earnings, and they help. But growth can't tell you where to buy, where you're wrong, or how many shares to buy. The chart does all three. A great company in a broken chart is still a broken chart.
questions.lesson_line: Numbers help. The chart decides.
questions.simple: False. The chart gives the entry, the stop and the size, so it comes first and growth is a plus.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h17)
rests on the owner's rulebook D40

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: EMA Crossback, a fresh reclaim
20 EMA pullback, old uptrend
Remount, the 50-day was lost
Bull flag, a pause after a run
questions.why: That's an EMA Crossback. Same line, different story. This stock was just in a decline. It got back over the 9 and 20 EMA a few sessions ago, and this pullback is its first test since. That's the crossback, and it has its own lesson. Our 20 EMA pullback is a leader that's been trending up for a while and comes back to a rising line. So before you name it, ask when the line got reclaimed.
questions.lesson_line: Ask when the line was reclaimed. A first test soon after is a crossback.

wrong.20 EMA pullback, old uptrend: Same line, but the averages were only just reclaimed. That first test is the crossback.
wrong.Remount, the 50-day was lost: A Remount retakes a 50-day or 200-day line it lost for days. This one reclaimed the 9 and 20 EMA.
wrong.Bull flag, a pause after a run: A flag comes after a sharp run up. This came out of a slide.

questions.story: This stock slid for weeks. A few sessions ago it closed back over its 9 and 20 EMA. Now it pulls back and tests the 20 EMA for the first time since.
questions.simple: It's the crossback. The stock just turned up out of a slide, while a pullback is a rest in an older uptrend.

deeper.trap: Both setups touch the same 20 EMA, so the charts can look alike. The tell is the order of events. Reclaimed recently, out of a slide, it's a crossback. A long-working uptrend makes it a pullback.

reasons: rests on D-002 and D-026 defaults
the card's session window is proposed and the Kell quote could not be fetched directly
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Which name fits?
choices: A Remount; a lost line retaken
A 20 EMA pullback, then a bounce
An undercut and rally of a line
An EMA Crossback; the first retest
questions.answer: A Remount; a lost line retaken
questions.why: A Remount. Five or more consecutive closes under a 50-day or 200-day line is a line lost. The close back above it is the retake. Nine closes in a row fits. A pullback allows at most one close under its line.
questions.lesson_line: Count the closes under the line. Five or more in a row, then back above it, is a Remount, not a pullback.

wrong.A 20 EMA pullback, then a bounce: A pullback allows at most one close under its line. This stock lost its 50-day for nine sessions.
wrong.An undercut and rally of a line: Nine closes in a row under the line is five or more, which the card calls a Remount.
wrong.An EMA Crossback; the first retest: A Crossback is the first retest of the averages after the stock has closed back above them. Today is the retake itself, not a retest.

questions.story: The stock closed under its 50-day for nine sessions in a row, then today closed back above it.
questions.simple: It is a Remount, because the stock lost its 50-day for many days in a row and then took it back.

deeper.trap: Counting closes under the wrong line. A pullback allows at most one close under the 20 EMA. A Remount is five or more closes in a row under a 50-day or 200-day line, then retaken. Two closes in a row under the 20 EMA already end the pullback setup, long before it could be a Remount.

reasons: the five-close count is a proposed card number

questions.q: Which name fits, and what decides it?
choices: Bull flag; the pole decides
20 EMA pullback; the line decides
EMA Crossback; the pop decides
No flag; the pole is under 30%
questions.why: A bull flag. A flag needs a pole, a gain of 20% or more inside 20 sessions, then a tight drift. This stock gained 24% in 12 sessions, then moved sideways five days. A 20 EMA pullback needs a session that tags the line, and this range sits well above it.
questions.lesson_line: A pole in front of a tight drift makes a flag. A pullback needs a session that tags the line.

wrong.20 EMA pullback; the line decides: A pullback needs a session whose low tags the line. This range sits well above it, and a pole stands in front. That is a flag.
wrong.EMA Crossback; the pop decides: A crossback follows a reclaim of the averages out of a decline. The story describes a 24% rise, not a reclaim.
wrong.No flag; the pole is under 30%: Kullamagi's 30% to 100% or more is the prior move for his own breakout setup. Our flag card needs a pole of 20% or more inside 20 sessions.

questions.story: The stock rose 24% in 12 sessions, then moved sideways in a tight range for five days. Its 20 EMA is still well below the range.
questions.simple: It is a bull flag, because the 24% rise in 12 sessions is a pole followed by a tight drift.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi wants a move of 30% to 100% or more before his own breakout setup. That is his filter, not our flag card, which needs a gain of 20% or more inside 20 sessions. Do not carry one number into the other's rule.

reasons: tied to held decision D-029
the 20% in 20 sessions pole is a proposed number
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Which name fits?
choices: The MAU&R costume of U&R
The 20 EMA pullback setup
A Remount of the lost line
No trade; any break kills it
questions.why: The undercut and rally in its moving-average costume. Ask what the buy is. On our current default, a low that undercut the 20 EMA, bought as the move back above the line, is the U&R. The pullback buys the intraday turn off a held line.
questions.lesson_line: Same line, different buy. Buying the move back through the line is the U&R, not the pullback.

wrong.The 20 EMA pullback setup: Its buy is the turn off a held line, such as red to green. Buying the move back above the line is the U&R.
wrong.A Remount of the lost line: The line was under water for two hours, not for five or more closes. That is an undercut, not a lost line.
wrong.No trade; any break kills it: The rules that end a setup count closes under the line, not intraday breaks. This buy is a different setup, the U&R.

questions.story: At 10 am the low breaks 1% under the 20 EMA. By noon price is back above the line and you buy the move back through it.
questions.simple: It is the undercut and rally, because the buy came as price moved back through the line.

deeper.trap: The same chart can be two setups. A shallow undercut can sit inside the pullback's touch band, so depth alone cannot name it. The buy names it. Buy the intraday turn off a held low and it is the pullback. Buy the move back through the line and it is the U&R.

reasons: rests on held decisions D-002, D-003 and D-036
keyed on provisional defaults that may change
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Are these 20 EMA pullbacks?
choices: No; not longs under the 200-day
Yes; the 20 EMA held both times
Yes, but at half the usual size
No; two holds in a month is too few
questions.why: No. We take no longs below the 200-day simple moving average unless it is a parabolic long. Both bounces happened under a falling 200-day, so they are bear-market bounces, not pullbacks in a trend. AlphaTrends puts it the other way: above the 200-day, the larger trend is innocent until proven guilty.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day a hold of the 20 EMA is a bounce. We do not buy bounces.

wrong.Yes; the 20 EMA held both times: The holds are real and the context is wrong. The 200-day rule is a hard line.
wrong.Yes, but at half the usual size: Size does not fix the context. No longs below the 200-day unless it is a parabolic long.
wrong.No; two holds in a month is too few: The count of holds is not the test. The test is the larger trend: no longs below the 200-day unless it is a parabolic long.

questions.story: In a bear market a stock bounces off its 20 EMA twice in a month. Both times price is under a falling 200-day.
questions.simple: No, because we do not buy longs below the 200-day, so a hold of the 20 EMA there is only a bounce.

deeper.trap: Two clean holds of the 20 EMA feel like proof. Under a falling 200-day they are bounces. The rule is no longs below the 200-day simple moving average unless it is a parabolic long, so check the 200-day before the 20 EMA.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (h10)
rests on the owner's rulebook B26
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: On our card, a stock above a 200-day that is lower than it was 20 sessions earlier still passes the context.
questions.why: False. The card's context line says the 200-day SMA is not lower than it was 20 sessions earlier. A 200-day that is lower fails it, even with price above it. A flat 200-day passes.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, and the 200-day not lower than 20 sessions ago. Both halves matter.
questions.simple: False, because the card wants the 200-day to be no lower than it was 20 sessions earlier.

deeper.counter: Above the 200-day is the rulebook line. The slope test is the card's own extra. A stock above a 200-day that is lower than 20 sessions ago passes the rulebook line but fails the card's context.

reasons: one cited fact carries the key (c08)
the 20 session slope test is a proposed number
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Is it still a setup?
choices: Yes, but the grade comes down
No, heavy selling voids it
Yes, volume makes no difference
No, wait for volume to dry up
questions.answer: Yes, but the grade comes down
questions.why: Yes, but grade it down. A heavy-volume red day into the line is a distribution day. Somebody big was selling, so be mindful of it. It doesn't void the setup though. The hold still closed above the line, so buyers defended it. I'd knock the grade down a notch, and a lower grade means a smaller size. INTC had a day like this at 2.3x its average volume.
questions.lesson_line: One loud red day into the line is a warning and a lower grade. It doesn't void the setup.

wrong.No, heavy selling voids it: It knocks the grade down. It doesn't kill the setup.
wrong.Yes, volume makes no difference: It does. Heavy selling into the line is a warning and a lower grade.
wrong.No, wait for volume to dry up: Volume isn't a must. It moves the grade up or down, and the hold already happened.

questions.story: A pullback to the rising 20 EMA holds and closes above the line. One of the down days on the way in ran 2.3x its 50-day average volume.
questions.simple: Yes, at a lower grade. Heavy selling is a warning, so you size it smaller instead of throwing it out.

deeper.trap: The loud red day is easy to read as a veto. It isn't. Don't wave it through either. Grade it down and size it smaller. INTC in 2017 had one on 2.3 times its average volume.

reasons: rests on the settled HEAVY-DOWN ruling (2026-11-14)
the 1.5x line is a card number

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Our limit on one stock is at most ___ tries in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.why: 3. At most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. Each try is a new trade on a new hold session, with its own trigger and stop.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week and six a month on one stock. That is the cap.
questions.simple: The most is 3 tries a week on one stock, and 6 in a month.

deeper.trap: The cap counts every try on one stock, and each try must be a new trade with its own trigger and stop. A stop-out is not a reason to skip the cap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E56
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Was that loss a mistake?
choices: No, the stop did what it's for
No, the close back up erased it
Yes, buy back at 546.88 and hold
Yes, a stop-out means a bad setup
questions.answer: No, the stop did what it's for
questions.why: No. The stop did exactly what it's for. The low at 538.05 traded through 540.97, and you were out with the loss you planned. 3.1% is a bit wider than I like, but it's inside our 5%. Yes, it ran to 610 without you. That stings. But nobody knew that at the low, and the stop can't know it either. A stop that only works when it's convenient isn't a stop. You'd buy it back only on a new trigger, as a new trade.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working, even when the stock runs after.

wrong.No, the close back up erased it: The stop fired when the low hit 538.05. A close back above doesn't undo the exit.
wrong.Yes, buy back at 546.88 and hold: Chasing back in isn't a trigger. You buy again only when it sets up again.
wrong.Yes, a stop-out means a bad setup: A stop-out doesn't make the setup bad. Judge the trade by the plan, not by what happened next.

questions.story: You bought a hold at 558.32 with your stop at 540.97, about 3.1% away. Next day it opens at 543.35, drops to 538.05 and stops you out. It closes at 546.88 and runs to 610 within a month.
questions.simple: No. The stop did its job, and a stock running after you're out doesn't make the exit wrong.

deeper.trap: Judging the trade by what came after. CAT closed at 546.88 and reached 610 within a month, but nobody knew that at the low of 538.05. A stop is judged by the plan, not the aftermath.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B21 and A4
3.1% stop width is held under D-005
one worked example

questions.q: Do you hold it through the report?
choices: No, we hold through only at 5R
No, the 3-day window bars it
Yes, it's close enough to 5R
Yes, a breakeven stop covers it
questions.answer: No, we hold through only at 5R
questions.why: No. We only hold through a report when the trade is up 5R. 3.9R isn't 5R, and close doesn't count. A report can gap the stock right past your stop overnight, and no stop catches that. At 5R you've got the cushion to sit through a bad gap. At 3.9R you don't, so you're out before the report. That's exactly where NVDA was here, and it cost us upside. I'll take that trade every time.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you can't stop. Five R buys the ticket. Almost doesn't.

wrong.No, the 3-day window bars it: That window is for new buys. Holding is the 5R test, and 3.9R falls short.
wrong.Yes, it's close enough to 5R: Close isn't 5R. The line is the line.
wrong.Yes, a breakeven stop covers it: A stop can't catch an overnight gap. That's why the 5R test exists.

questions.story: Your 20 EMA pullback buy peaked at 3.9R and has never been higher. The company reports tomorrow.
questions.simple: No. A report can gap it past your stop, and 3.9R isn't enough cushion to sit through that.

deeper.counter: This rule costs upside. NVDA's best run in our data was 25.1R, and the rule had us out under 5R before the report. We accept that cost to avoid a gap past the stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook B22

questions.q: The trigger is 45.00 and the stock opens at 46.62, above it. How far above the trigger is the open, in percent?
questions.why: The open's gain over the trigger is (46.62 minus 45.00) divided by 45.00, which is 3.6%. That is inside the 4% line, so the fill at the open is allowed. The stop stays under the hold candle, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap against the trigger. Inside 4% you may take the open.
questions.simple: The open is 3.6% above the trigger, which is under the 4% limit, so we may take the open.

deeper.trap: Inside 4% does not mean a free trade. The stop stays under the hold candle, so a higher fill widens the stop distance and the shares shrink. At 3.6% above the trigger the size is already smaller than planned.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook C28

wrong.103.6%: That is the open as a share of the trigger, not the gain.
wrong.162.0%: Turned the dollar gap into a percent without dividing by the trigger.

questions.q: What happens to the last third?
choices: Sold on the close under it
Held; the stop is at breakeven
Added to, buying the dip
Held to a fixed 8R target
questions.answer: Sold on the close under it
questions.why: Sold. Two thirds are banked at 3R and 5R. The last third trails the 10-day line for a fast mover or the 21-day for a steadier one. A close below the line is the exit.
questions.lesson_line: Two thirds banked, the last third on the trail. The close below the line is the exit.

wrong.Held; the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven is the floor, not the plan. The trail is the exit for the last third.
wrong.Added to, buying the dip: Full size at one price; no adding. A close under the trail is an exit, not an add.
wrong.Held to a fixed 8R target: The last third trails the line. There is no fixed target.

questions.story: You bought ILMN's hold at 95.90, stop 93.85. 3R came in 10 sessions and a third came off; 5R and another third. ILMN is a steady mover, so you trail its 21-day. Weeks later it closes under that line.
questions.simple: The last third is sold, because the stock closed under its 21-day trail line.

deeper.counter: Breakeven is only the floor under the last third. The trail is the plan: the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones, sold on a close below it. ILMN's best run reached 40.2R, so a fixed target of 8R would have sold far too soon.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook E51 and E52
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Before the trigger, the 20 EMA crosses under the 50-day. The pullback setup is off.
questions.why: True. I pass on it. We buy a leader resting on its 20 EMA, and a leader's 20 EMA sits over its 50-day. When the 20 crosses under, the short trend just rolled over under the medium one. That's a stock in repair, not a leader resting. A 20 EMA that flattens or turns down tells you the same thing. You check all of this before you buy. Once you're in, the stop and the trail handle the exit.
questions.lesson_line: The fast line under the slow line isn't a pullback. It's a trend in trouble.
questions.simple: True. A 20 EMA under the 50-day means the trend is weakening, so it's no longer a leader resting.

deeper.trap: The test is before the trigger. A cross after you're in is a different decision, and the stop and the trail handle that.
deeper.counter: Keller's proper order has the fast EMA over the 50-day, and the 50-day over the 200-day.

reasons: the cross test is a proposed card line

questions.q: What's the fix?
choices: Stop under the low, size from it
Keep the close stop, size for 4%
Use a real 1.5% stop, same size
Keep both, the line is a fine stop
questions.answer: Stop under the low, size from it
questions.why: Put a real stop a few cents under the hold session's low, then size from that. Two things are wrong here. A close under a line can't sit with your broker as an order. You'd be counting on yourself to sell at the bell, and that's exactly when people freeze. And you sized for 1.5% when your real exit is 4% away. One loss would cost you more than twice what you planned. Stop first, then the size. If the honest stop doesn't fit your risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: A line isn't an order. And you never pick the size before the stop.

wrong.Keep the close stop, size for 4%: Sizing for 4% helps, but a close under a line still isn't an order. The stop isn't real.
wrong.Use a real 1.5% stop, same size: Now the stop is set to fit the size. It sits inside the noise and gets hit. Stop first, then size.
wrong.Keep both, the line is a fine stop: A line is a place to watch. The stop is a price at your broker, a few cents under the low.

questions.story: You set your stop as a close under the 20 EMA, about 4% away. Then you size the trade as if the stop were only 1.5% away.
questions.simple: Put a real stop under the hold low and size from it, so a loss never costs more than you planned.

deeper.trap: Sizing off the stop you wish you had. The size comes from the real exit. With the real exit 4% away, a size built for 1.5% risks far more than you planned.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A3, A5 and D41

questions.q: Write the plan. Entry, stop, earliest sell?
choices: Buy 100.39, stop 99.07, sell day 3+
Limit on the 20 EMA, stop 95.00, hold
Buy the close, stop at 50-day, day 1
Buy 100.38, stop 99.10, all out at 5R
questions.why: Buy at market at 100.39, a cent over the 100.38 high. Stop at 99.07, a few cents under the 99.10 low. That's about 1.3% of risk, tight and clean. The hold candle isn't perfect. It has a long upper wick, so sellers leaned on it into the close. That's why you buy the trade over 100.38, not the close. The first sell is a judgment, and I'd rarely take it before day 3, because the money comes from a push over several days. This was GE. It reached 3R in 5 sessions. Write the plan the night before, set your alert at 100.38, and just execute it.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell, trail. Write it the night before, then just execute it.

wrong.Limit on the 20 EMA, stop 95.00, hold: A limit on the line buys before anything held. And 95.00 is nowhere near the candle's low.
wrong.Buy the close, stop at 50-day, day 1: The trigger is a trade over the high, not the close. A stop down at the 50-day is far wider than the hold low. And we very rarely sell on day 1.
wrong.Buy 100.38, stop 99.10, all out at 5R: The buy is a cent over the high and the stop a few cents under the low. And 5R isn't an all-out exit.

questions.story: The last bar holds the rising 20 EMA and closes above it. Its low is 99.10 and its high is 100.38.
questions.simple: Buy over the hold high, stop just under its low, and don't sell before day 3.

deeper.example: GE, January 2024: the low kissed the line to the cent, a 1.3% stop, and the stock reached 3R in 5 sessions. The stop may move up to breakeven as the trade works. The first sell is a judgment.

questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Pass, Orange means A+ setups only
Buy it, a clean hold is a hold
Buy it, Orange just halves size
Pass, Orange means all cash

The filter is a guide, but I'd respect it here.

wrong.Buy it, Orange just halves size: Orange narrows you to A+. A smaller size doesn't turn a B into an A+.
wrong.Pass, Orange means all cash: That's Red, mostly cash. Orange still buys the A+ setups.

questions.story: The app's market filter reads Orange. That's one step above Red, and the market is under real pressure. A leader holds its rising 20 EMA. Our grade, how clean the setup is, comes out B.
questions.simple: Pass. In a shaky market only the cleanest setups are worth the risk, and this one's a B.

questions.q: Do you take the trigger?
choices: Yes, it closed back over the line
Yes, any dip under the line is fine
No, any dip under the line kills it
No, it needs a second hold first
questions.answer: Yes, it closed back over the line
questions.why: Yes. That's a shakeout, not a lost line. Sellers pushed it under the 20 EMA and buyers took it right back by the close. I actually like that. The weak hands got flushed and the line still held. How deep a dip can go is a judgment call, not a fixed number. A shallow dip that closes back above is the easy case. CRM did exactly this and reached 3R in 2 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: A low under the line that closes back above it still counts as a hold.

wrong.Yes, any dip under the line is fine: Not any dip. How deep is a judgment call. This one was shallow and closed back above.
wrong.No, any dip under the line kills it: A dip under isn't an automatic fail. This one closed back above the line the same day.

questions.story: The hold session's low dips just under the 20 EMA. By the close it's back above the line. Next session it trades over that candle's high.

questions.q: Here's the hold session. Check the touch, the 50-day and the slope of the line. Do you take it or pass?
choices: Take it, the low hit the 20 EMA
Pass, the low reached the 50-day
Pass, the 20 EMA is falling
Take it, it held the 50-day
questions.answer: Take it, the low hit the 20 EMA
questions.why: Take it. The low kissed the rising 20 EMA to the cent, and the session closed above it. The 50-day sits underneath, untouched. And the line's pointed up. It was a four-day drift on 0.78x volume, quiet the whole way. The candle has a long upper wick, so it's not perfect. That's fine, because you only buy if it trades over that high. Your stop under that low was only 1.3% away. This was GE. It triggered the next day and hit 3R in 5 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Low on the line, close above it, 50-day below. That's the picture.

wrong.Pass, the low reached the 50-day: Look again. The 50-day runs under this low. The line it tagged is the 20 EMA.
wrong.Pass, the 20 EMA is falling: The 20 EMA is rising into the hold. A falling line would be a pass. This one isn't.
wrong.Take it, it held the 50-day: Right call, wrong line. The low never reached the 50-day. It held the 20 EMA.

questions.simple: Take it. The low reached the rising 20 EMA and closed above it, with the 50-day below.

deeper.example: GE, January 2024: a four-day drift on 0.78x volume, the low 0.02 ATR under the line. Buy 100.39, stop 99.07, a 1.3% stop. It reached 3R in 5 sessions, and the best run was 36.0R.

questions.q: The hold session. Which line did the low reach? Take it as a 20 EMA pullback or pass.
choices: Pass; the low went down to the 50-day
Take it; the 20 EMA line held up
Take it; both lines were tagged
Pass; the low never reached the 20 EMA
questions.answer: Pass; the low went down to the 50-day
questions.why: Pass as a 20 EMA pullback. The hold low of 401.01 sat under the 50-day SMA at 408.58, with the 20 EMA right beside it at 408.60. The low went through both lines, so the 20 EMA did not hold the dip, even though the close ended above them. That is the 50-day form, judged in its own lesson. It stopped, best 0.56R.
questions.lesson_line: Name the line the low touched before you name the setup.

wrong.Take it; both lines were tagged: The low did go through both lines, and that is the problem. A 20 EMA pullback's low must hold above the 50-day.
wrong.Take it; the 20 EMA line held up: The low went through the 20 EMA to the 50-day. The 20 EMA pullback's low holds above the 50-day.
wrong.Pass; the low never reached the 20 EMA: The low went through the 20 EMA and on to the 50-day. The 20 EMA sits almost on top of the 50-day here.

questions.simple: Pass, because the low fell through the 20 EMA to the 50-day, so this is the 50-day setup, not this one.

questions.q: A 20 EMA pullback stopped on day one for 1.3% to 2.5% is a loss the plan expected, not a broken rule.
questions.why: True. The failures in our data were all stopped on the first session with stops 1.3% to 2.5% wide; one ordinary red day took them. The stop is the exit, and the small loss is the cost of the tight stop.
questions.lesson_line: Tight stops get taken by noise sometimes. That is the price of the small loss.

questions.q: A leader you like trades 2.5 million shares a day on average. What's the most shares you'd ever own of it?
questions.why: 25,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. 1% of 2.5 million is 25,000. The reason: own too big a piece of the daily volume and you can't get out fast without pushing the price against yourself. That matters most on the day you need out. So treat it as a ceiling, whatever your risk math says.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the average daily volume. That's the ceiling.
questions.simple: 25,000. That's 1% of the daily volume, so you can still get out quickly.

questions.q: A clean 20 EMA pullback in a leader lifts our cap on how much of its daily volume we may own.

questions.q: What do you do with the buy alert?
questions.story: Monday held the 20 EMA, and your buy is a cent over Monday's high. Tuesday the stock sinks instead, and its low breaks the 50-day SMA without trading over Monday's high.
choices: Cancel it; the 20 EMA setup is off
Cancel it; any red day voids it
Keep it; Monday's hold counts
Raise it above Tuesday's high
questions.answer: Cancel it; the 20 EMA setup is off
questions.why: Cancel it. On our card, a low that breaks the 50-day before entry ends the 20 EMA pullback, and Monday's hold no longer counts. It is the 50-day pullback, if anything.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the 50-day before the buy and the 20 EMA pullback is off.

wrong.Keep it; Monday's hold counts: Monday held, but the break before the entry ends the setup. The 50-day pullback is a different card.
wrong.Raise it above Tuesday's high: A new buy level does not repair the break. The setup is off until it sets up again.
wrong.Cancel it; any red day voids it: Not every red day ends it. The low breaking the 50-day before the buy is what ends the 20 EMA setup.

questions.simple: Cancel it, because once the low breaks the 50-day before you buy, the 20 EMA pullback is over.

questions.q: Three tries on one stock this week, three stop-outs. It sets up a fourth time. What do you do?
choices: Skip it, you hit the week's limit
Take it, every try is a new trade
Take it, but at half size
Skip it till the month ends
questions.answer: Skip it, you hit the week's limit
questions.why: Skip it. We take at most 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock, and you've used this week's 3. Each try was its own trade, and that's fine. But a name that keeps stopping you out is telling you something. It's not ready, or it's not the one. The cap keeps a stubborn name from bleeding you with small loss after small loss. Look at it again next week if it's still acting right.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week, six a month on one stock. Then it's off the list.

wrong.Take it, every try is a new trade: Each try is a new trade, but the cap still counts them. After 3 in a week, you stop.
wrong.Take it, but at half size: A smaller size doesn't lift the cap. It's 3 tries a week, any size.
wrong.Skip it till the month ends: It's the weekly limit you hit. The month allows 6, so next week you can look again.

questions.simple: Skip it. Three tries a week is the cap, so a stock that keeps failing can't keep costing you.

questions.story: A leader ran from 60 to 80, then drifted six quiet sessions. Today its low of 74.60 touches the 20 EMA, which reads 74.30. That line read 71.20 ten sessions ago.
questions.q: How does the card read the 20 EMA here?
choices: Rising; above its level 10 sessions ago
Flat; price is under its high of 80
Weak; it did not rise on all 10 sessions
Not rising until price retakes 80
questions.answer: Rising; above its level 10 sessions ago
questions.why: Rising. The 20 EMA is rising when it is higher than it was 10 sessions earlier. Here it reads 74.30 against 71.20 ten sessions ago, so it passes. A pullback is price drifting down to a line that still climbs, so a price under the high of 80 is expected. Kullamagi has the leader surf its rising lines.
questions.simple: The line is higher than it was ten sessions ago, so it is rising, and the dip in price does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: Judge the line, not the price. A pullback sits under the high by design.

wrong.Flat; price is under its high of 80: The test looks at the line, not the price. A pullback sits under the swing high by design, so a price under 80 says nothing about the line.
wrong.Weak; it did not rise on all 10 sessions: The card compares the line today with its level 10 sessions earlier. It does not ask for a rise on every session.
wrong.Not rising until price retakes 80: The rising test needs nothing from the high of 80. Price retaking a high is a breakout, not part of this test.

questions.story: A leader peaked at 72.00. Since then it has moved sideways in a loose range for 22 sessions on light volume. Today its low tags the rising 20 EMA.
questions.q: Is this a 20 EMA pullback by our card?
choices: No; the drift ran too long for this card
Yes; a quiet drift of any length counts
Yes; only the touch of the line matters
No; it should last under 5 sessions
questions.answer: No; the drift ran too long for this card
questions.why: No. On our card the pullback lasts 2 to 15 sessions from the swing high to the hold session. This one has run 22, which is too long for this card. Our TOL example drifted 10 days to the line and still fit. Count the sessions before you judge the touch.
questions.simple: No, because a pullback here lasts at most 15 sessions, and this one has run 22.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions. A drift that long is a base, not a pullback.

wrong.Yes; a quiet drift of any length counts: Quiet volume helps the grade, but the card also limits the length. A drift of any length is not a pullback.
wrong.Yes; only the touch of the line matters: The touch is one part of the pattern. The pullback must also last 2 to 15 sessions from the swing high to the hold session.
wrong.No; it should last under 5 sessions: The card allows up to 15 sessions, not under 5. TOL drifted 10 days and still fit.

questions.story: A leader drifts six sessions into its rising 20 EMA. One red day on the way down traded 1.7 times its 50-day average volume. Today a session holds the line.
questions.q: How do you treat that heavy red day?
choices: Keep it; the heavy day lowers the grade
Drop it; heavy selling voids the setup
Grade it higher; volume shows interest
Ignore it; volume has no effect on grade
questions.answer: Keep it; the heavy day lowers the grade
questions.why: Keep it, at a lower grade. The card calls a down day on more than 1.5 times the 50-day average volume a distribution day to be mindful of. We treat volume as a grade, not a requirement. So this is a B- cue, not a veto. A quiet drift is an A+ cue. The hold session and the trigger still decide the buy.
questions.simple: Keep it, but grade it lower, because heavy selling into the line hurts the grade and does not end the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Volume grades the setup. It does not gate it.

wrong.Drop it; heavy selling voids the setup: Volume is not a requirement for the setup to count. A heavy red day lowers the grade. It does not void the setup.
wrong.Grade it higher; volume shows interest: Heavy selling into the line is a B- cue. Volume that raises the grade is quiet on the way down and heavier on the way up.
wrong.Ignore it; volume has no effect on grade: Volume does move the grade. A quiet pullback is an A+ cue and heavy selling into the line is a B- cue.

questions.q: What do you do with this one?
questions.story: A leader holds its 20 EMA. Your buy is a cent over the hold high, at 82.00. The hold low is 76.00, so your stop would sit at 75.97, about 7.4% under the buy.
choices: Wait for a tighter trigger
Take it, the size shrinks to fit
Take it, move the stop up to 3%
Take it, wide stops are fine
questions.why: Wait for a tighter trigger. I like a stop 1-3% under the buy. 3.5% is good, and about 5% is the most I'll take. This one's about 7.4%. Too wide. Sure, you could buy fewer shares. But a tighter trigger puts the stop closer, so the same risk buys more shares and a wrong trade gets cut sooner. Let it set up tighter. And never move the stop up just to make it fit.

wrong.Take it, the size shrinks to fit: The size does shrink. But past 5% we mostly wait, because a tighter trigger gets you more shares for the same risk.
wrong.Take it, move the stop up to 3%: That stop isn't honest. It sits inside the noise. Never move the stop just to fit the trade.
wrong.Take it, wide stops are fine: That's what the 5% line is for. Past it, we mostly wait.

questions.simple: Wait. A closer stop buys more shares for the same risk and cuts a wrong trade sooner.
questions.lesson_line: Past about 5% away, wait for a tighter trigger. Never pull the stop up to fit.
